claims.source: In both cases, the amplitude and half-duration of the action potentials elicited at 1 Hz were not significantly affected by the application of 30 µM ZD7288 (data not shown and Figure 4B and C, respectively), indicating that HCN channels do not alter the active membrane properties profoundly.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that ZD7288 does not significantly affect action potential amplitude and half-duration.

claims.claim: Blocking HCN channels significantly impaired the ability of mossy fibers to fire at high frequencies.
claims.source: Blocking HCN channels significantly impaired the ability of mossy fibers to fire at high frequencies (20 stimuli at 200–1666 Hz).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental recordings showing reduced failure-free firing frequency in the presence of ZD7288.

claims.claim: The average failure-free frequency in cerebellar mossy fibers was reduced from 854 ± 60 Hz under control conditions to 426 ± 63 Hz in the presence of ZD7288 (n = 20 and 10, respectively; PT-Test = 0.0002).
claims.source: The average failure-free frequency was reduced from 854 ± 60 Hz under control conditions to 426 ± 63 Hz in the presence of ZD7288 (n = 20 and 10, respectively; PT-Test = 0.0002; Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of failure-free firing frequency in cerebellar mossy fibers with and without ZD7288.

claims.claim: HCN channels ensure reliable high-frequency firing in cerebellar mossy fibers.
claims.source: These experiments show, that HCNs, despite their slow kinetics, ensure reliable high-frequency firing.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that blocking HCN channels impairs high-frequency firing.

claims.claim: ZD7288 caused a hyperpolarization of the resting membrane potential by, on average, 5.4 mV in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons.
claims.source: ZD7288 caused (i) a hyperpolarization of the resting membrane potential by, on average, 5.4 mV (–80.0 ± 0.6 mV and –85.4 ± 1.4 mV for control and ZD7288-treated cMFBs n = 94 and 35, respectively), (ii) a doubling of the apparent input resistance calculated from the steady-state voltage at the end of the current step (794 ± 48 MΩ and 1681 ± 185 MΩ, respectively), and (iii) a doubling of the apparent membrane time constant, as determined by a mono-exponential fit to the initial decay of the membrane potential (14.4 ± 0.8 ms and 35.0 ± 2.5 ms, respectively; see legend of Figure 5B for statistical testing).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of resting membrane potential in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons with and without ZD7288.

claims.claim: ZD7288 caused a doubling of the apparent input resistance in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons.
claims.source: ZD7288 caused (i) a hyperpolarization of the resting membrane potential by, on average, 5.4 mV (–80.0 ± 0.6 mV and –85.4 ± 1.4 mV for control and ZD7288-treated cMFBs n = 94 and 35, respectively), (ii) a doubling of the apparent input resistance calculated from the steady-state voltage at the end of the current step (794 ± 48 MΩ and 1681 ± 185 MΩ, respectively), and (iii) a doubling of the apparent membrane time constant, as determined by a mono-exponential fit to the initial decay of the membrane potential (14.4 ± 0.8 ms and 35.0 ± 2.5 ms, respectively; see legend of Figure 5B for statistical testing).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of apparent input resistance in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons with and without ZD7288.

claims.claim: ZD7288 caused a doubling of the apparent membrane time constant in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons.
claims.source: ZD7288 caused (i) a hyperpolarization of the resting membrane potential by, on average, 5.4 mV (–80.0 ± 0.6 mV and –85.4 ± 1.4 mV for control and ZD7288-treated cMFBs n = 94 and 35, respectively), (ii) a doubling of the apparent input resistance calculated from the steady-state voltage at the end of the current step (794 ± 48 MΩ and 1681 ± 185 MΩ, respectively), and (iii) a doubling of the apparent membrane time constant, as determined by a mono-exponential fit to the initial decay of the membrane potential (14.4 ± 0.8 ms and 35.0 ± 2.5 ms, respectively; see legend of Figure 5B for statistical testing).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of apparent membrane time constant in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons with and without ZD7288.

claims.claim: Adding cAMP in various concentrations to the intracellular solution depolarized the membrane potential and decreased both the input resistance and the apparent membrane time constant in a concentration-dependent manner in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons.
claims.source: Adding cAMP in various concentrations to the intracellular solution depolarized the membrane potential and decreased both the input resistance and the apparent membrane time constant in a concentration-dependent manner.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of membrane potential, input resistance, and membrane time constant with different cAMP concentrations, as shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: HCN channels in cerebellar mossy fibers determine the passive membrane properties as a function of the intracellular cAMP concentration.
claims.source: These data suggest that HCN channels in cerebellar mossy fibers determine the passive membrane properties as a function of the intracellular cAMP concentration.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that cAMP concentration affects membrane potential, input resistance, and membrane time constant.

claims.claim: Immunogold electron microscopy revealed only background immunoreactivity for HCN1 in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons.
claims.source: At the electron microscopic level, we found only background immunoreactivity for HCN1 (data not shown) but significant labeling for HCN2 (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunogold electron microscopy experiments showing no significant HCN1 labeling.

claims.claim: Immunogold electron microscopy revealed significant labeling for HCN2 in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons.
claims.source: At the electron microscopic level, we found only background immunoreactivity for HCN1 (data not shown) but significant labeling for HCN2 (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunogold electron microscopy experiments showing significant HCN2 labeling, as illustrated in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: HCN2 immunogold particles were diffusely distributed along the plasma membrane of cerebellar mossy fiber boutons, with similar labeling density in the adjacent mossy fiber axon.
claims.source: HCN2 immunogold particles were diffusely distributed along the plasma membrane of cMFBs, with similar labeling density in the adjacent mossy fiber axon (Figure 6B), which could be traced back up to 3.5 µm from cMFBs.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunogold electron microscopy showing diffuse distribution of HCN2 particles, as illustrated in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: HCN2 was uniformly distributed in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons without apparent spatial relations to synapses.
claims.source: HCN2 was uniformly distributed without apparent spatial relations to those synapses.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by 3D reconstruction of a cerebellar mossy fiber bouton showing uniform HCN2 distribution, as illustrated in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: The mean density of immunogold particles for HCN2 in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons was 22.7 ± 2.4 per μm2 (n = 6 cMFBs from two mice).
claims.source: The mean density of immunogold particles for HCN2 was 22.7 ± 2.4 per μm2 (n = 6 cMFBs from two mice).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of immunogold labeling density in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons.

claims.claim: HCN2 is the dominant subunit mediating Ih in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons.
claims.source: These data indicate that HCN2 is the dominant subunit mediating Ih in cMFBs, consistent with its pronounced cAMP-dependence.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the immunogold electron microscopy results showing significant HCN2 labeling and no significant HCN1 labeling, combined with the observed cAMP-dependence.

claims.claim: Hyperpolarizing voltage steps evoked a slowly activating, non-inactivating inward current in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons, which was inhibited by ZD7288.
claims.source: Hyperpolarizing voltage steps evoked a slowly activating, non-inactivating inward current, which was inhibited by ZD7288 (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by voltage-clamp recordings from cerebellar mossy fiber boutons showing slowly activating, non-inactivating inward currents that are blocked by ZD7288, as illustrated in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: The mean V½ of Ih activation in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons was –103.3 ± 0.8 mV (n = 36).
claims.source: Using the tail currents of ZD7288-sensitive currents evoked by voltage steps between –80 mV and –150 mV from a holding potential of –70 mV, we calculated the activation curve of Ih with a mean V½ of –103.3 ± 0.8 mV (Figure 7B; n = 36 V½-values, each from a different cMFB).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by voltage-clamp recordings and analysis of tail currents in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons.

claims.claim: About 7% of the overall HCN2-mediated current is active at rest in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons.
claims.source: On the basis of the average resting membrane potential of cMFBs, this means that about 7% of the overall HCN2-mediated current is active at rest.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the V½ of Ih activation and the average resting membrane potential of cerebellar mossy fiber boutons.

claims.claim: With 1 mM cAMP, V½ of Ih activation shifted by 17 mV to, on average, –86.6 ± 1.2 mV (n = 16 cMFBs; PT-Test <10−10).
claims.source: With 1 mM cAMP, V½ shifted by 17 mV to, on average, –86.6 ± 1.2 mV (n = 16 cMFBs; PT-Test <10−10; Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by voltage-clamp recordings from cerebellar mossy fiber boutons with 1 mM cAMP in the intracellular solution.

claims.claim: The EC50 of intracellular cAMP for HCN channels in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons is 40.4 µM.
claims.source: The resulting average shifts of V½ revealed an EC50 of 40.4 µM intracellular cAMP (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of V½ shifts at different cAMP concentrations, as shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: The endogenous cAMP concentration in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons is estimated to be 12.6 µM, with a 68% confidence interval of 1.8 to 60.7 µM cAMP.
claims.source: This voltage shift (4.9 ± 1.2 mV, n = 10 cMFBs) indicates an endogenous cAMP concentration of 12.6 µM in cMFBs, with a 68% confidence interval of 1.8 to 60.7 µM cAMP (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from perforated patch recordings showing a voltage shift compared to whole-cell recordings, combined with the EC50 of cAMP.

claims.claim: Under perforated patch conditions, the V½ of Ih in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons was –96.4 ± 1.2 mV (n = 10), significantly more depolarized than the corresponding whole-cell recordings after rupture of the perforated patch (–101.3 ± 1.0 mV; n = 10; PT-Test = 0.0076).
claims.source: Under perforated patch conditions, the V½ of Ih was –96.4 ± 1.2 mV (n = 10), significantly more depolarized than the corresponding whole-cell recordings after rupture of the perforated patch (–101.3 ± 1.0 mV; n = 10; PT-Test = 0.0076; Figure 7C; see Materials and methods for comparisons with additional control groups).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by perforated patch and whole-cell recordings from cerebellar mossy fiber boutons showing a significant difference in V½.

claims.claim: The reversal potential of Ih in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons was –23.4 ± 1.4 mV (n = 7).
claims.source: Furthermore, we estimated the reversal potential of Ih with short voltage ramps as described previously (Cuttle et al., 2001) and found a value of –23.4 ± 1.4 mV (n = 7; Figure 8C), similar to previous estimates (Aponte et al., 2006; Cuttle et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements using voltage ramps, as shown in Figure 8C, and is consistent with previous estimates from cited studies.

claims.claim: The depolarization caused by HCN2 channels brings the resting membrane potential closer to the threshold for voltage-gated Na+ channel activation, which accelerates the initiation of the action potential.
claims.source: In principle, the depolarization caused by HCN2 channels will bring the resting membrane potential closer to the threshold for voltage-gated Na+ channel activation, which could accelerate the initiation of the action potential (see discussion).
claims.evidence: The claim is a mechanistic explanation based on the known properties of HCN2 channels and voltage-gated Na+ channels.

claims.claim: The computational model predicted a decrease of the conduction velocity when the control HH model of Ih was removed, and conversely an increase with the 1-mM-cAMP-HH model.
claims.source: Interestingly, the models predicted a decrease of the conduction velocity when the control HH model was removed, and conversely an increase with the 1-mM-cAMP-HH model (Figure 9E), that was similar in extent to that measured experimentally with ZD7288 and 8-Br-cAMP treatments (cf. Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 9E, which are consistent with experimental data from Figure 1.

claims.claim: HCN2 channel modulation suffices to tune conduction velocity bidirectionally.
claims.source: These findings support our conclusion that HCN2 channel modulation suffices to tune conduction velocity bidirectionally.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the computational modeling results showing that changes in HCN2 channel activity can both increase and decrease conduction velocity.

claims.claim: The Vm-model but not the Rm-model caused an increase in conduction velocity, indicating that the depolarizing effect of axonal HCN2 channels determines conduction velocity.
claims.source: The results showed that the Vm-model but not the Rm-model caused an increase in conduction velocity, indicating that the depolarizing effect of axonal HCN2 channels determines conduction velocity (Figure 9E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results comparing the Vm-model and Rm-model, as shown in Figure 9E.

claims.claim: Increasing the resting membrane potential from –90 mV to –65 mV decreased the availability of voltage-dependent Na+ channels but increased the conduction velocity.
claims.source: Interestingly, increasing the resting membrane potential from –90 mV to –65 mV, decreased the availability of voltage-dependent Na+ (NaV) channels but increased the conduction velocity (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The conduction velocity decreased only at resting membrane potentials above –65 mV in the computational model.
claims.source: The conduction velocity decreased only at resting membrane potentials above –65 mV in our model.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The depolarization mediated by HCN2 channels accelerates the conduction velocity by bringing the membrane potential closer to the firing threshold.
claims.source: Together, these data indicate that the depolarization mediated by HCN2 channels accelerates the conduction velocity by bringing the membrane potential closer to the firing threshold.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the computational modeling results showing that the Vm-model increases conduction velocity.

claims.claim: It is approximately 100% more expensive to maintain the resting membrane potential with Ih than without or by depolarization alone (Vm-model).
claims.source: Computational modeling showed that it is ~100% more expensive to maintain the resting membrane potential with Ih than without or by depolarization alone (Vm-model; Figure 9F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling of metabolic costs, as shown in Figure 9F.

claims.claim: The metabolic cost of maintaining the resting membrane potential with Ih for one second was approximately 3-fold higher than the cost of generating one action potential.
claims.source: Furthermore, the metabolic cost of maintaining the resting membrane potential with Ih for one second was ~3-fold higher than the cost of generating one action potential (Figure 9F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling of metabolic costs, as shown in Figure 9F.

claims.claim: Assuming an average frequency of cerebellar mossy fibers of 4 Hz in vivo, the HCN2 channels increased the required energy of cerebellar mossy fibers by approximately 30%.
claims.source: Assuming an average frequency of cerebellar mossy fibers of 4 Hz in vivo (Chadderton et al., 2004; Rancz et al., 2007), the HCN2 channels increased the required energy of cerebellar mossy fibers by ~30%.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from computational modeling of metabolic costs combined with cited estimates of average firing frequency in vivo.

claims.claim: HCN2 channels are a major consumer of the energetic demands of axons.
claims.source: These data indicate that HCN2 channels are a major consumer of the energetic demands of axons.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the computational modeling results showing high metabolic costs of HCN2 channels.

claims.claim: HCN channels increase action potential velocity and fidelity in central axons.
claims.source: Here, we demonstrate that the HCN channels increase action potential velocity and fidelity in central axons.
claims.evidence: The claim summarizes the main findings of the study, supported by experimental data on conduction velocity and high-frequency firing.

claims.claim: HCN channels can change the arrival time of the action potential by, for example, 0.5 ms in the case of unmyelinated cerebellar parallel fibers (assuming 3 mm length and 0.3 m/s velocity).
claims.source: Although the changes in baseline conduction velocity are relatively small, considering the long distances that axons traverse in the brain, HCN channels can be expected to change the arrival time of the action potential by, for example, 0.5 ms in the case of unmyelinated cerebellar parallel fibers (assuming 3 mm length and 0.3 m/s velocity; Swadlow and Waxman, 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the measured changes in conduction velocity and cited estimates of axon length and velocity.

claims.claim: The cAMP-HCN pathway provides neuromodulators with an opportunity to finely tune energy consumption and temporal delays across axons in the brain.
claims.source: These results suggest that the cAMP-HCN pathway provides neuromodulators with an opportunity to finely tune energy consumption and temporal delays across axons in the brain.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental and modeling results showing that neuromodulators can modulate conduction velocity and that HCN channels have significant metabolic costs.

claims.claim: HCN channels are expressed in the heart and nervous system and comprise four members (HCN1–HCN4), which differ in their kinetics, voltage-dependence and degree of sensitivity to cyclic nucleotides such as cAMP.
claims.source: HCN channels are expressed in the heart and nervous system and comprise four members (HCN1–HCN4), which differ in their kinetics, voltage-dependence and degree of sensitivity to cyclic nucleotides such as cAMP (Biel et al., 2009; Robinson and Siegelbaum, 2003).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on HCN channels.

claims.claim: Membrane hyperpolarization activates HCN channels and causes a depolarizing mixed sodium/potassium (Na+/K+) current.
claims.source: Membrane hyperpolarization activates HCN channels and causes a depolarizing mixed sodium/potassium (Na+/K+) current.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about HCN channel function.

claims.claim: In the heart, the current through HCN channels (If) mediates the acceleratory effect of adrenaline on heart rate by direct binding of cAMP.
claims.source: In the heart, the current through HCN channels (If) mediates the acceleratory effect of adrenaline on heart rate by direct binding of cAMP (DiFrancesco, 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study on HCN channels in the heart.

claims.claim: In neurons, the current through HCN channels (Ih) controls a wide array of functions, such as rhythmic activity and excitability.
claims.source: In neurons, the current through HCN channels (Ih) controls a wide array of functions, such as rhythmic activity (Pape and McCormick, 1989) and excitability (Tang and Trussell, 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on HCN channels in neurons.

claims.claim: HCN channels are expressed throughout various subcellular compartments of neurons.
claims.source: In addition to the somatic impact, HCN channels are expressed throughout various subcellular compartments of neurons (Nusser, 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study on HCN channel expression.

claims.claim: Patch-clamp recordings from dendrites in pyramidal neurons have revealed particularly high densities of HCN channels that act to control the local resting potential and leak conductance, thereby playing important roles in regulating synaptic integration.
claims.source: For example, patch-clamp recordings from dendrites in pyramidal neurons have revealed particularly high densities of HCN channels that act to control the local resting potential and leak conductance, thereby playing important roles in regulating synaptic integration (George et al., 2009; Harnett et al., 2015; Kole et al., 2006; Magee, 1999; Williams and Stuart, 2000).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on dendritic HCN channels.

claims.claim: Ih seems to control the strength of synaptic transmission in the crayfish and the Drosophila neuromuscular junction.
claims.source: Ih seems to control the strength of synaptic transmission in the crayfish and the Drosophila neuromuscular junction (Beaumont and Zucker, 2000; Cheung et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on Ih in invertebrate neuromuscular junctions.

claims.claim: Presynaptic recordings from the vertebrate calyx of Held in the auditory brainstem found Ih to only have a marginal effect on neurotransmitter release.
claims.source: However, presynaptic recordings from the vertebrate calyx of Held in the auditory brainstem found Ih to only have a marginal effect on neurotransmitter release (Cuttle et al., 2001), but to exert a strong influence on the resting membrane potential (Cuttle et al., 2001; Kim and von Gersdorff, 2012) and on vesicular neurotransmitter uptake (Huang and Trussell, 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on Ih in the calyx of Held.

claims.claim: At the synaptic terminals of pyramidal neurons in the cortex of mice, HCN channels inhibit glutamate release by suppressing the activity of T-type Ca2+ channels.
claims.source: At the synaptic terminals of pyramidal neurons in the cortex of mice, HCN channels inhibit glutamate release by suppressing the activity of T-type Ca2+ channels (Huang et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study on HCN channels in cortical synaptic terminals.

claims.claim: In axons of the stomatogastric nervous system of lobsters, the action potential conduction was affected by dopamine acting via axonal HCN channels.
claims.source: Indeed, in axons of the stomatogastric nervous system of lobsters (Marder and Bucher, 2001), the action potential conduction was affected by dopamine acting via axonal HCN channels (Ballo et al., 2010; Ballo et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on HCN channels in lobster axons.

claims.claim: Studies on action potential propagation by Waxman and coworkers indicated that Ih counteracts the hyperpolarization of the membrane potential during periods of high-frequency firing.
claims.source: In vertebrates, studies on action potential propagation by Waxman and coworkers indicated that Ih counteracts the hyperpolarization of the membrane potential during periods of high-frequency firing (Baker et al., 1987; Birch et al., 1991; Waxman et al., 1995), and that it participates in ionic homeostasis at the node of Ranvier (Waxman and Ritchie, 1993).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by Waxman and colleagues.

claims.claim: Ih is crucial for the emergence of persistent action potential firing in axons of parvalbumin-positive interneurons.
claims.source: More recent investigations found Ih to be crucial for the emergence of persistent action potential firing in axons of parvalbumin-positive interneurons (Elgueta et al., 2015), but Ih seems to have an opposing effect on the excitability at the axon initial segment, where its activation reduces the probability of action potential initiation (Ko et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study on Ih in parvalbumin-positive interneurons.

claims.claim: There is evidence from extracellular recordings that blocking Ih decreases the action potential conduction velocity in unmyelinated central axons and peripheral axons of vertebrates.
claims.source: Finally, there is evidence from extracellular recordings that blocking Ih decreases the action potential conduction velocity in unmyelinated central axons (Baginskas et al., 2009; Soleng et al., 2003) and peripheral axons of vertebrates (Grafe et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on Ih and conduction velocity.

claims.claim: The neuromodulation of conduction velocity and the underlying cellular membrane mechanisms are not known in vertebrate axons.
claims.source: However, the neuromodulation of conduction velocity and the underlying cellular membrane mechanisms are not known in vertebrate axons.
claims.evidence: The claim identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study aims to address.

claims.claim: Cerebellar mossy fibers can conduct trains of action potentials at frequencies exceeding 1 kHz.
claims.source: However, cerebellar mossy fibers can conduct trains of action potentials at frequencies exceeding 1 kHz (Ritzau-Jost et al., 2014), making them an ideal target to investigate the impact of axonal HCNs on the propagation of high-frequency action potentials.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study on cerebellar mossy fibers.

claims.claim: The subunits HCN1 and HCN2 are predominantly expressed in the cerebellar cortex.
claims.source: Of the four HCN subunits (HCN1–HCN4), the subunits HCN1 and HCN2 are predominantly expressed in the cerebellar cortex (Notomi and Shigemoto, 2004; Santoro et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on HCN subunit expression in the cerebellum.

claims.claim: Previous studies in the cortex, hippocampus, and auditory brainstem primarily detected HCN1 in axons.
claims.source: Previous studies in the cortex, hippocampus, and auditory brainstem primarily detected HCN1 in axons (Elgueta et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2011; Ko et al., 2016), but HCN2 was found to be more sensitive to cAMP than HCN1 (Wang et al., 2001; Zagotta et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on HCN subunit expression in axons.

claims.claim: HCN2 was found to be more sensitive to cAMP than HCN1.
claims.source: Previous studies in the cortex, hippocampus, and auditory brainstem primarily detected HCN1 in axons (Elgueta et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2011; Ko et al., 2016), but HCN2 was found to be more sensitive to cAMP than HCN1 (Wang et al., 2001; Zagotta et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on HCN subunit cAMP sensitivity.

claims.claim: Temporal delays in the sub-millisecond domain will influence information processing in the central nervous system, because spike-timing dependent plasticity, coincidence detection, and the neuronal rhythms of cell ensembles precisely tune the arrival times of action potentials.
claims.source: Such temporal delays will influence information processing in the central nervous system, because spike-timing dependent plasticity (Caporale and Dan, 2008), coincidence detection (Softky, 1994), and the neuronal rhythms of cell ensembles (Buzsáki et al., 2013) precisely tune the arrival times of action potentials.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on spike-timing dependent plasticity, coincidence detection, and neuronal rhythms.

claims.claim: The diameter and the degree of myelination of cerebellar climbing fibers are tuned to offset the different arrival times of action potentials with a temporal precision of approximately 100 µs.
claims.source: There are several examples of the specific tuning of conduction velocity in the sub-millisecond domain: the diameter and the degree of myelination of cerebellar climbing fibers (Sugihara et al., 1993; Lang and Rosenbluth, 2003; but see Baker and Edgley, 2006), the degree of myelination of thalamocortical axons (Salami et al., 2003), and the internode distance of auditory axons (Ford et al., 2015) are all tuned exactly to offset the different arrival times of action potentials with a temporal precision of ~100 µs.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on conduction velocity tuning in various axons.

claims.claim: The cerebellum is involved in the accurate control of muscle contraction with a temporal precision of 1–100 ms.
claims.source: The cerebellum is involved in the accurate control of muscle contraction with a temporal precision of 1–100 ms (Hore et al., 1991).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study on cerebellar function.

claims.claim: Submillisecond correlations in spike timing occurring between neighboring Purkinje cells have been noted previously.
claims.source: Submillisecond correlations in spike timing occurring between neighboring Purkinje cells have been noted previously (reviewed in Isope et al., 2002; Person and Raman, 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous reviews on Purkinje cell spike timing.

claims.claim: Submillisecond precision of the mossy or parallel fiber input are critical for information processing in the cerebellar circuits.
claims.source: Furthermore, submillisecond precision of the mossy or parallel fiber input are critical for information processing in the cerebellar circuits (Braitenberg et al., 1997; Heck et al., 2001; Isope et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on cerebellar information processing.

claims.claim: The view of the axon as a cable-like compartment in which conduction velocity is static has substantially changed over recent years in favor of a model that allows flexibility and complex forms of axonal computation.
claims.source: Indeed, the view of the axon as a cable-like compartment in which conduction velocity is static has substantially changed over recent years in favor of a model that allows flexibility and complex forms of axonal computation (Debanne et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous review on axonal computation.

claims.claim: Axon diameters change during long-term potentiation.
claims.source: Recent findings showed that axon diameters change during long-term potentiation (Chéreau et al., 2017), and changes in myelination in the motor cortex were resolved during the learning of complex motor skills (McKenzie et al., 2014; for environmental effects on myelination see also Forbes and Gallo, 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study on axon diameter changes.

claims.claim: Changes in myelination in the motor cortex were resolved during the learning of complex motor skills.
claims.source: Recent findings showed that axon diameters change during long-term potentiation (Chéreau et al., 2017), and changes in myelination in the motor cortex were resolved during the learning of complex motor skills (McKenzie et al., 2014; for environmental effects on myelination see also Forbes and Gallo, 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on myelination changes during learning.

claims.claim: The control of conduction velocity is solely mediated by changes in resting membrane potential.
claims.source: Our analysis revealed that the control of conduction velocity is solely mediated by changes in resting membrane potential.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the computational modeling results showing that the Vm-model but not the Rm-model affects conduction velocity.

claims.claim: Isolated changes in membrane conductance and thus in the membrane time and length constant had no effect on conduction velocity.
claims.source: Isolated changes in membrane conductance and thus in the membrane time and length constant had no effect on conduction velocity (Figure 9E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 9E.

claims.claim: The increased conduction velocity upon depolarization is consistent with a previously observed correlation between conduction velocity and the depolarization from the resting potential required to reach the firing threshold in motoneurons.
claims.source: The increased conduction velocity upon depolarization is consistent with a previously observed correlation between conduction velocity and the depolarization from the resting potential required to reach the firing threshold in motoneurons (Carp et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study on conduction velocity in motoneurons.

claims.claim: Na+ channels have a steep steady-state inactivation and are partially inactivated at the resting membrane potential in axons.
claims.source: On the other hand, Na+ channels have a steep steady-state inactivation and are partially inactivated at the resting membrane potential in axons (Battefeld et al., 2014; Engel and Jonas, 2005; Rama et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on Na+ channel inactivation in axons.

claims.claim: The modeling results showed that increasing the membrane potential from –90 to –60 mV increased the conduction velocity despite significantly decreasing Na+ channel availability.
claims.source: However, our modeling results showed that increasing the membrane potential from –90 to –60 mV increased the conduction velocity despite significantly decreasing Na+ channel availability (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The modeling results are in agreement with the nonlinear cable theory predicting that the difference between the resting membrane potential and the firing threshold is a critical parameter for action potential conduction velocity.
claims.source: Interestingly, these findings are in agreement with the nonlinear cable theory predicting that the difference between the resting membrane potential and the firing threshold is a critical parameter for action potential conduction velocity (see, for example, Figure 12.25 in Jack et al. (1983) which shows increasing velocity with increasing safety factor, that is, decreasing excitation threshold 'VB').
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous theoretical work on cable theory.

claims.claim: The evolutionary design of HCN channels as a continuously open shunt for Na+ influx incurs significant metabolic costs.
claims.source: Our modeling results (Figure 9) indicate that the evolutionary design of HCN channels as a continuously open shunt for Na+ influx incurs significant metabolic costs.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the computational modeling results showing high metabolic costs of HCN channels.

claims.claim: A metabolically cheaper way to depolarize the membrane would be the expression of fewer Na+-K+-ATPases, resulting in a depolarized K+ reversal potential.
claims.source: These high costs might appear surprising, because a metabolically cheaper way to depolarize the membrane would be the expression of fewer Na+-K+-ATPases, resulting in a depolarized K+ reversal potential (cf. Vm-model in Figure 9).
claims.evidence: The claim is a theoretical consideration based on the computational modeling results.

claims.claim: The half-maximal shift of the activation of HCN2 channels occurs at a cAMP concentration of 40 µM.
claims.source: Using direct whole-cell recordings and immunogold EM from en passant boutons in cerebellar axons, we identified near exclusive expression of HCN2 isoforms and a half-maximal shift of the activation of HCN2 channels at a cAMP concentration of 40 µM (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of HCN2 activation at different cAMP concentrations, as shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: The perforated patch-recordings from axonal compartments provide the first direct estimate of endogenous cAMP concentration in vertebrate central axons of 13 µM.
claims.source: Furthermore, our perforated patch-recordings from axonal compartments provide, to our knowledge, the first direct estimate of endogenous cAMP concentration in vertebrate central axons of 13 µM (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by perforated patch recordings from cerebellar mossy fiber boutons, as shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: Previous estimates of endogenous cAMP concentration were 50 nM in Aplysia sensory neurons and 1 µM in cardiomyocytes.
claims.source: This is higher than previous estimates of 50 nM in Aplysia sensory neurons (Bacskai et al., 1993; but see Greenberg et al., 1987) and 1 µM in cardiomyocytes (Börner et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on cAMP concentration in other cell types.

claims.claim: A recently reported low cAMP-sensitivity of protein kinase A argues for high intracellular cAMP concentrations.
claims.source: But a recently reported low cAMP-sensitivity of protein kinase A (Koschinski and Zaccolo, 2017), a prototypical cAMP-regulated protein, also argues for high intracellular cAMP concentrations.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study on protein kinase A cAMP sensitivity.

claims.claim: A high endogenous cAMP concentration and expression of the HCN2 isoform facilitates the ability of neuromodulators to control conduction velocity bidirectionally and dynamically.
claims.source: A high endogenous cAMP concentration and expression of the HCN2 isoform facilitates the ability of neuromodulators to control conduction velocity bidirectionally and dynamically.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing high endogenous cAMP concentration and HCN2 expression, combined with the observed neuromodulation of conduction velocity.

claims.claim: Adenosine has been shown to be an endogenous sleep factor.
claims.source: Interestingly, adenosine, which decreased the conduction velocity (Figure 2), has been shown to be an endogenous sleep factor (Basheer et al., 2004; Porkka-Heiskanen et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on adenosine as a sleep factor.

claims.claim: Serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine play important regulatory functions during sleep in the cerebellum.
claims.source: Moreover, serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine play important regulatory functions during sleep in, for example, the cerebellum (Canto et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study on neuromodulators during sleep.

claims.claim: The cAMP-HCN pathway in axons could contribute to the reduced energy consumption of the brain during sleep.
claims.source: The cAMP-HCN pathway in axons could thus contribute to the reduced energy consumption of the brain during sleep (Boyle et al., 1994; Townsend et al., 1973).
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the observed effects of neuromodulators on conduction velocity and metabolic costs, supported by citations to previous studies on brain energy consumption during sleep.

claims.claim: Significant alterations of HCN channel expression and/or function have been described in pathologies such as stroke, porphyria, diabetic neuropathy, neuropathic pain, and inflammation.
claims.source: Significant alterations of HCN channel expression and/or function have been described in pathologies such as stroke (Jankelowitz et al., 2007), porphyria (Lin et al., 2008), diabetic neuropathy (Horn et al., 1996), neuropathic pain (Chaplan et al., 2003), and inflammation (Momin and McNaughton, 2009), as well as in a vertebrate model of demyelination (Fledrich et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on HCN channels in various pathologies.

claims.claim: HCN channels seem to be causally related to pain symptoms.
claims.source: Furthermore, HCN channels seem to be causally related to pain symptoms (Chaplan et al., 2003; Momin and McNaughton, 2009) and therapeutic blockade of HCN channels are also considered (Wickenden et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on HCN channels and pain.

claims.claim: HCN could play a compensatory role in restoring conduction velocity in some diseases.
claims.source: On the basis of our findings, HCN could also play a compensatory role in restoring conduction velocity in some diseases.
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the findings of the current study.

results.result: HCN channel blocker ZD7288 decreased conduction velocity by 4-9% in myelinated and unmyelinated central axons, while cAMP analog 8-Br-cAMP increased conduction velocity by 4-6%, demonstrating bidirectional control of conduction velocity by HCN channels.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 and C5-C7 provide consistent experimental evidence across three different axon types (mossy fibers, parallel fibers, optic nerves) showing bidirectional modulation of conduction velocity. Statistical testing is referenced in Figure 1, sample sizes are adequate (n=4-17), and the effects are consistent in direction across preparations. Claim C8 appropriately summarizes these findings.

results.result: At 30 µM concentration, ZD7288 did not affect voltage-dependent Na+ currents in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons, ruling out off-target effects on Na+ channels.
results.evaluation: Claim C4 is supported by recordings from 53 cMFBs showing no change in Na+ current amplitude or kinetics (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). This control experiment is critical for interpreting the conduction velocity results, as some studies have reported off-target effects of ZD7288 on Na+ channels.

results.result: Physiological neuromodulators bidirectionally modulate conduction velocity in cerebellar parallel fibers: norepinephrine increased velocity by 1.9%, while serotonin, dopamine, and adenosine decreased velocity by 3.5-7.2%.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C12 provide experimental data with adequate sample sizes (n=5-13) showing differential effects of neuromodulators on conduction velocity. The results are consistent with known receptor distributions and signaling pathways (Gs vs Gi coupling). However, the authors acknowledge using high concentrations (200 µM) and potential off-target effects, which introduces some uncertainty about physiological relevance.

results.result: The effects of cAMP and neuromodulators on conduction velocity are mainly mediated by HCN channels, as demonstrated by blocking experiments with ZD7288.
results.evaluation: Claim C14 is supported by experiments (Figure 2F-G) showing that pre-application of ZD7288 abolishes the effects of neuromodulators and 8-Br-cAMP on conduction velocity. The control experiments are well-designed, though the authors appropriately note that other cAMP-dependent channels could contribute.

results.result: Cerebellar mossy fiber boutons exhibit a substantial voltage sag (sag ratio 0.497 ± 0.030 at -150 mV) in response to hyperpolarizing currents, indicating the presence of Ih.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C16 are supported by current-clamp recordings (Figure 3B-C) with adequate sample size (n=12). The voltage sag is a well-established hallmark of HCN channel activity, and the quantification is appropriate.

results.result: HCN channels do not significantly alter the amplitude or half-duration of action potentials elicited at 1 Hz in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C18 are supported by experimental data (Figure 4B-C) showing no significant effects of ZD7288 on action potential properties at low frequency. This is an important control demonstrating that HCN channels primarily affect passive rather than active membrane properties under these conditions.

results.result: Blocking HCN channels with ZD7288 reduced the failure-free firing frequency in cerebellar mossy fibers from 854 Hz to 426 Hz, demonstrating that HCN channels ensure reliable high-frequency firing.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C21 are supported by experimental data (Figure 4D-E) with adequate sample sizes (n=10-20) and significant p-value (0.0002). The approximately 50% reduction in maximal firing frequency is substantial and physiologically relevant. Additional data on action potential broadening and amplitude reduction support the conclusion.

results.result: HCN channels determine passive membrane properties of cerebellar mossy fiber boutons in a cAMP-dependent manner: ZD7288 hyperpolarized resting potential by 5.4 mV and doubled input resistance and membrane time constant, while cAMP had opposite effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C26 are supported by extensive experimental data (Figure 5) with large sample sizes (n=35-94 for ZD7288, various n for cAMP concentrations). The effects are consistent and concentration-dependent for cAMP. Statistical testing shows p<10^-10 for all three parameters, indicating robust effects.

results.result: Immunogold electron microscopy revealed that HCN2 is the dominant subunit in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons and axons, with uniform distribution (22.7 ± 2.4 particles/µm²) and no significant HCN1 labeling.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C32 are supported by immunogold EM data (Figure 6) from 6 cMFBs from two mice. The 3D reconstruction provides strong evidence for uniform distribution. The density measurement is quantitative and includes appropriate controls for non-specific labeling (3.9% background). The conclusion about HCN2 dominance is well-supported.

results.result: Voltage-clamp recordings revealed slowly activating, non-inactivating Ih currents in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons with V½ of -103.3 mV, indicating approximately 7% of HCN2 channels are active at rest.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C35 are supported by voltage-clamp data (Figure 7A-B) with large sample size (n=36). The characterization of Ih is thorough, including kinetics and voltage-dependence. The calculation of 7% activation at rest is appropriately derived from the V½ and average resting potential.

results.result: HCN2 channels in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons show strong cAMP sensitivity (EC50 = 40.4 µM), and perforated patch recordings estimate endogenous cAMP concentration at 12.6 µM (68% CI: 1.8-60.7 µM).
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C39 are supported by systematic measurements at different cAMP concentrations (Figure 7B-D) with adequate sample sizes (n=10-16). The perforated patch approach is appropriate for estimating endogenous cAMP without dialysis. However, the wide confidence interval (1.8-60.7 µM) indicates substantial uncertainty in the endogenous cAMP estimate. The authors appropriately acknowledge this limitation and discuss potential for local cAMP compartments.

results.result: The reversal potential of Ih in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons was -23.4 ± 1.4 mV, consistent with a mixed Na+/K+ conductance.
results.evaluation: Claim C40 is supported by voltage ramp measurements (Figure 8C) with adequate sample size (n=7) and is consistent with previous estimates from cited studies. This parameter is important for the computational modeling.

results.result: Computational modeling revealed that HCN2 channels control conduction velocity solely through depolarization of resting membrane potential, not through changes in membrane conductance, as demonstrated by comparing Vm-model and Rm-model predictions.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C44, C47, C81-C82 are supported by systematic computational modeling (Figure 9E) that reproduces experimental observations. The dissection of depolarization vs. conductance effects using Vm-model and Rm-model is elegant and provides mechanistic insight. The model predictions match experimental data from Figure 1, strengthening the conclusions.

results.result: Computational modeling showed that increasing resting membrane potential from -90 to -65 mV increased conduction velocity despite decreasing Na+ channel availability, with velocity decreasing only above -65 mV.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C46 and C85 are supported by computational modeling (Figure 9—figure supplement 1). This counterintuitive result is important for understanding the mechanism. However, the authors appropriately note that the exact threshold depends on model assumptions about Na+ channel properties and density.

results.result: Computational modeling revealed that HCN2 channels are metabolically expensive: maintaining resting potential with Ih costs ~100% more than without Ih, ~3-fold more per second than one action potential, and increases total energy requirements by ~30% at 4 Hz firing.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C51 are supported by computational modeling of ATP consumption (Figure 9F). The calculations are based on Na+ influx and appear methodologically sound. The comparison to action potential costs and the frequency-dependent analysis provide important context. However, these are model predictions that would benefit from experimental validation.

results.result: HCN channels increase action potential velocity and fidelity in central axons, can change arrival times by ~0.5 ms in parallel fibers, and provide neuromodulators an opportunity to tune energy consumption and temporal delays.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C54 synthesize the major findings of the study. C52 is well-supported by the experimental data on conduction velocity and high-frequency firing. C53's calculation of 0.5 ms delay is appropriately derived from measured velocity changes and cited axon dimensions. C54 is a reasonable inference from the combined experimental and modeling results, though it remains somewhat speculative regarding physiological function.

results.result: The mechanism by which HCN2 channels accelerate conduction velocity is consistent with nonlinear cable theory: depolarization brings membrane potential closer to firing threshold, which is more important than the negative effect of increased Na+ channel inactivation.
results.evaluation: Claims C41, C83, and C86 provide theoretical context for the modeling results. The consistency with cable theory (Jack et al. 1983) and previous observations in motoneurons (Carp et al. 2003) strengthens the mechanistic interpretation. However, these are theoretical explanations that depend on model assumptions.

results.result: Background claims about HCN channel properties, distribution, and functions in various systems, establishing context for the current study.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C72 are background/introduction claims supported by appropriate citations to previous literature. These establish the context and knowledge gaps that motivate the current study. C68 specifically identifies the gap in knowledge about neuromodulation of conduction velocity in vertebrate axons.

results.result: Background claims about the importance of precise timing in neural circuits and examples of conduction velocity tuning in various systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C80 provide important context from the literature about the functional significance of sub-millisecond timing precision and examples of anatomical tuning of conduction velocity. These are well-supported by citations and establish the physiological relevance of the findings.

results.result: Discussion of Na+ channel inactivation properties and metabolic considerations regarding HCN channel function.
results.evaluation: Claims C84 and C87 are supported by citations and modeling results. C88 is a theoretical consideration about alternative mechanisms for depolarization, appropriately presented as speculation. These claims provide important context for interpreting the modeling results.

results.result: Summary of key findings on HCN2 cAMP sensitivity and endogenous cAMP concentration, with comparison to previous estimates and discussion of implications for neuromodulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C93 synthesize experimental findings (EC50 = 40 µM, endogenous cAMP = 13 µM) and compare to previous literature. The comparison shows the current estimate is higher than previous estimates in other systems. C92 provides additional support from recent literature on PKA sensitivity. C93 is a reasonable inference about the functional implications.

results.result: Speculation that the cAMP-HCN pathway in axons could contribute to reduced brain energy consumption during sleep, based on the role of adenosine and other neuromodulators in sleep regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C95 are supported by citations about neuromodulators and sleep. However, C96 is explicitly speculative and lacks direct experimental evidence. While the speculation is reasonable given the metabolic costs of HCN channels and the effects of sleep-related neuromodulators, it remains a hypothesis requiring future testing.

results.result: Discussion of HCN channel alterations in various pathologies and speculation about potential compensatory roles in disease.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C98 are supported by citations to previous studies on HCN channels in pathology. However, C99 is explicitly speculative about a compensatory role for HCN channels in restoring conduction velocity in disease, lacking direct experimental evidence from the current study.

results.result: HCN channel blocker ZD7288 decreased conduction velocity by 4-9% in myelinated cerebellar mossy fibers, unmyelinated parallel fibers, and optic nerves, while cAMP analog 8-Br-cAMP increased conduction velocity by 4-6% in the same preparations, demonstrating that HCN channels control conduction velocity in both myelinated and unmyelinated central axons.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raised concerns about the specificity of ZD7288 and requested occlusion experiments or antagonist controls (Essential Revision 3). In the second round, Reviewer 2 noted that occlusion experiments in Figure 3 showed 3-4% ZD-insensitive changes comparable to neuromodulator effects, stating 'these experiments are only partially successful in demonstrating specificity of neuromodulatory action on HCN channels.' The imperfect selectivity of ZD7288 and incomplete occlusion leave uncertainty about whether all observed effects are solely HCN-mediated.

results.result: At 30 µM concentration, ZD7288 did not affect Na+ currents in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons, as demonstrated by recordings from 53 boutons showing no change in amplitude or kinetics.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge this control experiment. The data address known concerns about ZD7288 off-target effects on Na+ channels, and no reviewer questioned the validity of these findings.

results.result: Neuromodulators bidirectionally modulate conduction velocity in cerebellar parallel fibers: norepinephrine increased velocity by 1.9%, while serotonin, dopamine, and adenosine decreased it by 3.5-7.2%. These effects are mainly mediated by HCN channels, as demonstrated by occlusion experiments with ZD7288.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 expressed concern about high neuromodulator concentrations (200 µM) and potential off-target effects, requesting antagonist experiments to confirm specificity (Essential Revision 1). In the second round, Reviewer 2 noted that occlusion experiments showed 3-4% ZD-insensitive changes, stating 'it would seem that these experiments are only partially successful in demonstrating specificity' and asking 'What is explanation for the remaining ZD-insensitive neuromodulation?' Both reviewers requested expanded discussion of neuromodulatory mechanisms and off-target possibilities.

results.result: Current-clamp recordings from cerebellar mossy fiber boutons show a substantial voltage 'sag' in response to hyperpolarizing currents, with a sag ratio of 0.497 at approximately -150 mV, indicating the presence of Ih.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these electrophysiological characterizations of Ih. The data are consistent with established HCN channel properties and support the presence of functional HCN channels in these terminals.

results.result: ZD7288 application did not significantly affect the amplitude and half-duration of action potentials elicited at 1 Hz in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons, indicating that HCN channels do not profoundly alter active membrane properties.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not question these findings. The data help clarify that HCN effects on conduction velocity are not mediated through changes in action potential waveform at low frequencies.

results.result: Blocking HCN channels with ZD7288 significantly impaired high-frequency firing in mossy fibers, reducing failure-free frequency from 854 Hz to 426 Hz, demonstrating that HCN channels ensure reliable high-frequency firing despite their slow kinetics.
results.evaluation: In the second round, Reviewer 1 noted these new recordings in Figure 5 are 'impressive and highlight an interesting aspect of HCN function in axons, contributing to reliability during high frequency trains,' and commented that 'AP failures at high frequency may be more consequential than these small changes in timing.' Reviewers accepted these findings as demonstrating an important functional role for HCN channels.

results.result: ZD7288 caused 5.4 mV hyperpolarization and doubled both input resistance and membrane time constant in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons. Adding cAMP in various concentrations depolarized the membrane and decreased input resistance and time constant in a concentration-dependent manner, indicating that HCN channels determine passive membrane properties as a function of intracellular cAMP concentration.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these passive membrane property measurements. The data provide important mechanistic insight into how HCN channels affect axonal excitability and are consistent with known HCN channel biophysics.

results.result: Immunogold electron microscopy revealed only background HCN1 immunoreactivity but significant HCN2 labeling (22.7 particles/µm²) diffusely distributed along the plasma membrane of cerebellar mossy fiber boutons and adjacent axons, indicating that HCN2 is the dominant subunit mediating Ih in these structures.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge the immunogold EM data. The identification of HCN2 as the predominant subunit is consistent with the observed cAMP sensitivity and provides important molecular specificity to the findings.

results.result: Voltage-clamp recordings revealed slowly activating, non-inactivating inward currents blocked by ZD7288, with V½ of activation at -103.3 mV (control) shifting to -86.6 mV with 1 mM cAMP. The EC50 for cAMP is 40.4 µM, and approximately 7% of HCN2-mediated current is active at rest.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these biophysical characterizations. The data provide detailed mechanistic insight into HCN2 channel properties in axons and are consistent with known HCN2 pharmacology.

results.result: Perforated patch recordings revealed endogenous cAMP concentration in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons of 12.6 µM (confidence interval 1.8-60.7 µM), representing the first direct estimate of endogenous cAMP in vertebrate central axons, based on a 4.9 mV depolarizing shift in V½ compared to whole-cell recordings.
results.evaluation: Reviewers praised these technically challenging experiments. Reviewer 2 noted 'The data set also includes a number of impressive, technically challenging experiments, such as perforated patch-clamp recordings from mossy fiber terminals and estimations of cAMP concentration in the terminal.' The findings were accepted as providing novel insight into axonal cAMP levels.

results.result: The reversal potential of Ih in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons was -23.4 mV, measured using voltage ramps and consistent with previous estimates.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge this measurement, which is consistent with established values for HCN channels and supports the mixed cation conductance of these channels.

results.result: Computational modeling demonstrated that HCN2 channel modulation suffices to tune conduction velocity bidirectionally, with the depolarizing effect (Vm-model) but not changes in membrane conductance (Rm-model) determining conduction velocity by bringing the membrane potential closer to firing threshold.
results.evaluation: Reviewers requested more detailed exploration of the modeling (Essential Revision 2). Reviewer 2 asked to 'explore this aspect in more detail to see how robust this result is across a range of conditions' and to 'report relative NaV availability in each model.' In the second round, Reviewer 2 acknowledged 'The modeling better explores the impact of HCN channels on Na channel availability,' but the initial concerns about robustness across conditions and the interaction with Na+ channel inactivation suggest some remaining uncertainty about the completeness of the mechanistic explanation.

results.result: Computational modeling showed that increasing resting membrane potential from -90 to -65 mV decreased Na+ channel availability but increased conduction velocity, with velocity decreasing only above -65 mV, demonstrating that proximity to threshold dominates over Na+ channel availability in determining conduction velocity.
results.evaluation: In the second round, Reviewer 2 noted 'The modeling better explores the impact of HCN channels on Na channel availability,' indicating that the authors adequately addressed the requested analysis of Na+ channel inactivation effects. The counterintuitive finding that depolarization increases velocity despite reducing Na+ availability is now supported by the modeling.

results.result: Computational modeling revealed that maintaining resting potential with Ih is ~100% more expensive than without Ih, costs ~3-fold more per second than generating one action potential, and increases total energy requirements of cerebellar mossy fibers by ~30% at 4 Hz firing, indicating HCN2 channels are major consumers of axonal energy.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge the metabolic cost calculations. These findings provide important context for understanding the evolutionary trade-offs of using HCN channels for conduction velocity modulation.

results.result: HCN channels increase action potential velocity and fidelity in central axons, can change arrival times by ~0.5 ms in unmyelinated parallel fibers, and the cAMP-HCN pathway provides neuromodulators with an opportunity to tune energy consumption and temporal delays across brain axons.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 questioned the functional significance, noting 'The differences in conduction velocity are small, and on a sub-millisecond time scale' and asking 'What is the evidence for the significance of submillisecond timing in the cerebellum? The mossy fiber input is ultimately low-pass filtered by granule cells with very slow membrane time constants' (Essential Revision 1). While reviewers acknowledged the phenomenon exists, concerns about biological relevance and the magnitude of in vivo modulation remain, with Reviewer 2 stating in round 2 'The magnitude of HCN channel modulation on conduction velocity in vivo remains to be determined.'

results.result: High endogenous cAMP concentration (12.6 µM) and expression of the HCN2 isoform facilitate the ability of neuromodulators to control conduction velocity bidirectionally and dynamically.
results.evaluation: This integrative claim depends on the neuromodulator experiments (C9-C14), which reviewers found only partially convincing due to incomplete occlusion and lack of antagonist controls. The high cAMP concentration and HCN2 expression are well-supported, but the extent to which this enables physiological neuromodulation remains uncertain.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate the same claims (C1-C3, C5-C8) about bidirectional modulation of conduction velocity across three axon types. OpenEval finds the evidence SUPPORTED with consistent experimental results and adequate statistics. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN due to concerns about ZD7288 specificity and incomplete occlusion in neuromodulator experiments (3-4% ZD-insensitive changes), questioning whether all effects are solely HCN-mediated.

Both evaluate C4 regarding Na+ current controls. Both find this SUPPORTED - OpenEval notes it addresses known ZD7288 off-target concerns, and peer reviewers did not challenge these control experiments.

Both evaluate neuromodulator effects (C9-C13). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED despite acknowledging high concentrations and potential off-target effects. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, expressing concerns about 200 µM concentrations, requesting antagonist experiments, and noting incomplete occlusion (3-4% ZD-insensitive changes). OpenEval R3 covers C9-C13 while Peer R3 includes C14.

OpenEval R4 evaluates C14 (ZD7288 pre-application abolishing neuromodulator effects) as SUPPORTED. Peer R3 includes C14 within broader neuromodulator evaluation rated UNCERTAIN due to incomplete occlusion and specificity concerns. Partial overlap in claims but different scopes of evaluation.

Both evaluate C15-C16 regarding voltage sag as HCN hallmark. Both find SUPPORTED - OpenEval notes adequate sample size and appropriate quantification; peer reviewers did not challenge these electrophysiological characterizations.

Both evaluate C17-C18 regarding lack of ZD7288 effects on action potential properties at low frequency. Both find SUPPORTED - OpenEval emphasizes this as important control for passive vs active properties; peer reviewers accepted these findings without challenge.

Both evaluate C19-C21 regarding maximal firing frequency reduction. Both find SUPPORTED - OpenEval notes substantial 50% reduction with strong statistics; peer reviewers praised these as 'impressive' findings highlighting HCN function in high-frequency reliability, with Reviewer 1 noting AP failures may be more consequential than timing changes.

Both evaluate C22-C26 regarding passive membrane properties. Both find SUPPORTED - OpenEval notes extensive data with large sample sizes and robust statistics; peer reviewers did not challenge these measurements and accepted them as providing mechanistic insight.

Both evaluate C27-C32 regarding immunogold EM and HCN2 distribution. Both find SUPPORTED - OpenEval emphasizes quantitative density measurements and HCN2 dominance; peer reviewers accepted the data without challenge and noted consistency with cAMP sensitivity.

Both evaluate Ih characterization but with different claim coverage. OpenEval R10 covers C33-C35 (voltage-clamp characterization) rated SUPPORTED. Peer R9 covers C33-C37 (including cAMP effects) also rated SUPPORTED, with reviewers not challenging the biophysical characterizations.

Both evaluate endogenous cAMP estimation. OpenEval R11 covers C36-C39 rated SUPPORTED despite wide confidence intervals. Peer R10 covers C38-C39, C90 rated SUPPORTED, with reviewers praising the technically challenging perforated patch experiments. Partial overlap with both acknowledging technical difficulty and novel insights.

Both evaluate C40 regarding reversal potential measurement. Both find SUPPORTED - OpenEval notes consistency with previous literature and importance for modeling; peer reviewers did not challenge this measurement.

Both evaluate computational modeling of HCN effects on conduction velocity. OpenEval R13 covers C42-C44, C47, C81-C82 rated SUPPORTED, emphasizing elegant dissection of mechanisms. Peer R12 covers C41-C44, C47, C81-C82 rated UNCERTAIN, with reviewers requesting more detailed exploration of robustness and Na+ channel availability, though acknowledging improvements in second round.

Both evaluate C45-C46, C85 regarding counterintuitive depolarization effects on velocity. OpenEval finds SUPPORTED while noting model-dependent thresholds. Peer reviewers find SUPPORTED after second round revisions, with Reviewer 2 noting 'The modeling better explores the impact of HCN channels on Na channel availability.'

Both evaluate C48-C51 regarding ATP consumption calculations. Both find SUPPORTED - OpenEval notes methodologically sound calculations with important context; peer reviewers did not challenge the metabolic cost analysis.

Both evaluate C52-C54 regarding functional significance and timing precision. OpenEval finds SUPPORTED while noting C54 remains somewhat speculative. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, questioning biological relevance given sub-millisecond scale, low-pass filtering by granule cells, and noting 'The magnitude of HCN channel modulation on conduction velocity in vivo remains to be determined.'

OpenEval R17 evaluates C41, C83, C86 (theoretical context for modeling) as SUPPORTED but model-dependent. Peer R12 includes C41 within broader modeling evaluation rated UNCERTAIN. Minimal overlap with different evaluation scopes.

OpenEval R18 evaluates C55-C72 (background/introduction claims) as SUPPORTED by appropriate literature citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found - these contextual claims were not separately evaluated by reviewers.

OpenEval R19 evaluates C73-C80 (literature context on timing precision and anatomical tuning) as SUPPORTED by citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found - these background claims establishing physiological relevance were not separately evaluated by reviewers.

OpenEval R20 evaluates C84, C87-C88 (theoretical considerations about alternative mechanisms) as SUPPORTED. No corresponding peer review evaluation found - these contextual modeling considerations were not separately evaluated by reviewers.

Both evaluate claims about physiological neuromodulation capacity. OpenEval R21 covers C89-C93 rated SUPPORTED, synthesizing EC50 and endogenous cAMP findings. Peer R16 evaluates only C93 rated UNCERTAIN, noting this depends on neuromodulator experiments that showed incomplete occlusion. Minimal overlap with different evaluation scopes and conclusions.

OpenEval R22 evaluates C94-C96 (speculation about sleep-related neuromodulation) as UNCERTAIN, noting C96 is explicitly speculative without direct evidence. No corresponding peer review evaluation found - this speculative discussion was not separately evaluated by reviewers.

OpenEval R23 evaluates C97-C99 (speculation about compensatory role in disease) as UNCERTAIN, noting C99 lacks direct experimental evidence. No corresponding peer review evaluation found - this speculative discussion was not separately evaluated by reviewers.
